title: The Lamp Book of the Bell Yard
author: the Fellowship of Lamp-Makers and Lighters of Whisper-Grove; kept by Osmer Lowry, warden
origin: the lamp-makers' loft, Bell Yard, Whisper-Grove
summary: The ordinances, rounds and yearly remembrances of the Grove's lamplighters, kept by an old warden for the nephew who will have the book after him.
text: Osmer Lowry, warden of the Fellowship of Lamp-Makers and Lighters, his book; which is to say the Fellowship's book, while he keeps it. After him it goes to Kitto Lowry, his sister's boy, as soon as Kitto can trim a wick without saying a word his mother would not like.
THE ORDINANCES OF THE FELLOWSHIP, as they were read to me when I was bound, and as I have read them to every boy and girl bound since.

First. A lamp of the Grove is lit at dusk and not before, whatever the Moot says about winter afternoons. The pools light the faces; the lamps light the way. Until the pools come on, the willows give light enough, and oil is dear.

Second. Every lighter knows his round by heart and by count, so that he could walk it blind; and every lighter walks his round the same way every night, at the same pace, so that a child who is lost at dusk has only to stand under a lamp and wait, and the lighter will come by within the hour and know her.
Third. No lamp is left half-lit. A lamp that is begun is finished, or it is put out and begun again. A lamp half-lit is a promise half-kept.

Fourth. The lamp at the Moot-house door burns all night while the Moot is sitting. The lighter of that round sits up with it on the steps, and may listen, and may not speak, for in that room he is not a householder, only the lamp-man.

Fifth. On the night the Grove's water is highest, the Fellowship gives paper and wax and wick for the basin lanterns to anyone who asks, at no charge, and no lighter is to ask whose name the lantern is for.

Sixth. Whoever lights the last lamp of his round says, Goodnight, Grove, not loud. Nobody knows when this began. It is an ordinance because a warden once tried to strike it as foolishness and the Fellowship sat in the loft until morning and would not let him.

THE ROUNDS. There are nine rounds in the Grove, and the Ashlane is the longest because of the steps. The Bell Yard round is the oldest and the shortest: eleven lamps on iron arms, from the Moot-house corner down past the joiners' shops to the turn, and back along the other side to the plaza, so that the lighter ends where he began. By custom the warden keeps it for himself. I have kept it since 396, and my father before me.
REMEMBRANCES. A warden writes a line a year, or more if the year deserves it.
396. Made warden, nine hands to two. The two were right; I was too young.

398. New oil up from the Reach, rape oil, cheaper than willow-oil, and it smokes. The Moot complained of the smell. We mixed it half and half and told nobody, and the Moot stopped complaining. Write that down, Kitto: the Moot complains of what it knows.
401. Kitto bound to me at nine years old. He asked me whether lamps were afraid of the dark. I told him a lamp is the only thing in the Grove that is not, and that is the whole of the trade.
404. Kitto burned off both eyebrows on the Ashlane round and lit the rest of the round anyway. Fined a penny for language. Paid it himself, and did not argue, which is more than I did at his age.

407. The water highest in thirty years. We gave out four thousand papers and ran short of wick by the ninth hour of the evening. A little girl came for a lantern for her grandmother and could not say the name for crying, so her brother said it for her, and the people on the steps said it after him, as they do. Ordinance Five. I did not ask.
409. The colour of the flame, written here so the book remembers it if I do not. At the Moot-house door on a still night the flame is the yellow of a pear in Sheafmonth, with blue at the root.

412. The Screaming Year. The Fellowship's book ought to know, so I write it. Since the sky went wrong in the south, the flame is not the colour it was. Same oil. Same wicks. Every lighter over thirty says it, and the young ones look at us as though we were simple. It is paler. A pear in Firstfruit, not in Sheafmonth. The Moot has ordered the lighters to go quietly on the rounds, no calling and no whistling, because singing in other places has begun to bring things. We have always gone quietly. A lighter who has to be told to be quiet has never lit a lamp.

413. The Moot asked whether the lamps ought to be left dark, so as not to be seen from outside. The Fellowship met in the loft and voted to keep lighting, eleven hands to none. I said to the Moot, A lit street is a street where somebody is expected home. They let it stand.

414. My knees. Kitto has the Bell Yard round, though it is the warden's by custom, and I walk behind him and tell him what he is doing wrong. He does nothing wrong. I tell him anyway. That is also custom.

415. Kitto made journeyman at Canopy, fourteen hands to none, and the old ones banged the table. He says he means to marry. I have told him a lamp-man's wife sees him at dusk and at dawn and never in between, and he says that is twice a day more than most men manage.

415, later. I have taken the Bell Yard round back for the winter while Kitto does the Ashlane, which wants young knees. Eleven lamps down, eleven back, and the plaza at the end of it with the pools coming on. I find I minded watching more than I mind the knees. It is the best walk in the Grove and I would not give it to anybody.
Kitto. When this book is yours, keep the Ordinances, and add to them if you must, and never strike the sixth. Light the lamps whether or not anyone is coming. Somebody always is.
notes: Written before the Unnaming (last entry 415), so nothing of 416 is known; the reader brings the irony. Canon: Book One Ch14 (the Weeping Plaza, colonnade and Moot-house, the basin where the city floated lamps on festival nights, the Bell Yard), Ch15 (an old lamplighter going along Bell Yard lighting dry lamps and, at the end of the row, turning round and coming back to the first; the pools lighting from below). The book does not say that the Hollow lamplighter is its author; a player may wonder. Series Bible Part III (everyone over thirty remembers when red was redder) and Part V (412, the Screaming Year); Part IV (the Narrow; hymns bring hounds). Vol VII (b) §4 (the Drowned Lanterns: one lantern per name, read aloud, the night the Grove's water is highest); Vol VII §2 and §4 (months; Canopy, first Memoryday of Ashfall). Vol II Realm VII (lilac pools lighting faces from the chin; courteous Grove speech). Names grepped in js/ and story/ and the other batches (Osmer, Lowry, Kitto: no hits; Lowry is only a substring of flume_lowrings). title: The Day-Book of a Midwife of the Ashlane
author: Grisel Imrie, midwife, of the Ashlane
summary: Two years of births in the Ashlane, set down by a brisk and loving midwife: the hard nights, the naming on the water, and the count she means to finish one day.
text: Grisel Imrie, midwife, of the Ashlane, her day-book, begun in Stillmonth 414 because the last one is full. If found, return it to the house with the blue door at the top of the steps. If I am out, I am at somebody's bedside. Leave it on the step and the cat will mind it.

For whoever comes after me and was not raised in the Grove: we keep our names on the eighth day. The child is carried down to the nearest pool and its name is said over the water three times, once by the mother, once by whoever stands for the father, and once by the midwife, so that the Grove has heard it from three mouths and will not let it go. The Church's man says the custom is harmless. Nobody asked him.

3 Stillmonth 414. The cooper's wife at the top of the lane. A girl, seven pounds and a bit, the fourth hour of the night, and she came out shouting at the cold, which is right and proper. I sang her down low, the way we all do now, and put her to the breast, and the shouting stopped, and her father sat on the stairs and wept. There are no hounds in the Ashlane and there never have been. But since the Screaming Year every father in the Grove listens to his own child as though it were a bell rung in the street, and I do not blame them.

11 Stillmonth. Said on the water: Petronel. The mother said it, the grandmother stood for the father, who is away with the willow-cutters until spring, and I said it third. The pool showed the grandmother a kitchen none of us knew, which she says is a good sign. I said that every sign is a good sign after a safe birth, and she said that was not how signs worked, and we were both right.
Thawmonth. Nine this month and every one of them whole. I am too old to write that without touching wood, so I have touched the table.

Reedmonth. A first child at the fuller's, a boy, eleven hours of it, and the mother so frightened of being heard that she would not push. I said to her, dear one, you may shout at me all you like. Whatever is out there is listening for singing, and nobody in the history of the world has ever mistaken this for singing. She laughed, and then she pushed. Said on the water on the eighth day: Bede. A good plain name. He will grow into it.
Firstfruit. Hot. The pools steam at dusk. I have told every mother due this month to sit with her feet in a basin and her opinions to herself, and none of them will do either.

14 Longsun 415. The fuller's girl again, her second lying-in, and it was two. The first came roaring. The second came blue and still, and would not take a breath, and I did everything there is: the cold water and the warm, the rubbing, my own mouth over its face. The old women say a child that will not cry is a door left open. I do not hold with sayings. I hold the child upside down.

For a long minute it would not. Then the first one, in her mother's arms across the room, roared again, very loud and very rude, and the second one opened its eyes and roared straight back at her. Would not be outdone. In thirty-one years I have never seen anything so like a sister. Said on the water: Columb and Sabra. I said both names twice over, to make up for the fright, and nobody stopped me.

Dustmonth. A girl from the Cloister choir came to my door to ask whether babies can hear singing before they are born, because the choir-mistress had told them so. I said yes, but that mostly what they hear is their mothers' stomachs. She was disappointed in me. I told her to sing to her aunt's belly anyway, softly, because it would do the aunt good whatever it did for the baby.

Harvestmonth. Fourteen this month. I am tired in a way that sleep does not mend. I have taken a girl from the Bell Yard to carry the bag and learn. She is good with mothers and hopeless with fathers, which is the right way round.

Lambmonth 416. The lamp-man's boy from the Bell Yard has married, and his wife is expecting at the back end of the year, and they came to me together to ask what they ought to be doing. I said: nothing, and less of it. He is to keep the lamps lit on the stair. She is to eat.

Sheafmonth 416. Two clerks of the Office came up the steps with a great book for the register, very civil, with gloves on, and asked for every child I have brought since 400, with the date and the house and the voice. I asked what they meant by the voice. They said: the cry, whether high or low, strong or thin. I said that a cry is a cry, and that I do not write down how a baby sounds any more than I write down how it smells, which is lovely. They wrote that down, word for word. I gave them the names, because a name is not mine to keep back. I did not give them this book.

Sheafmonth, later. The works at the end of the Bell Yard go all night now, a grinding you feel in your teeth more than hear, and it comes up the lane when the wind is wrong. The mothers ask me whether it will harm the babies. I tell them babies have heard worse, and I believe it, and I do not like it either.

I have counted tonight, for no reason except that the lamp was good and the kettle was on. Since I was seventeen and held my first one for my mother: one thousand and ninety-one, and every one of them said on the water. When I am too old to kneel I mean to sit at the top of the Ashlane steps of a morning and count the ones who go by and say good morning, little mother. I expect it will take me the whole day.
notes: Written before the Unnaming of Ashfall 416; the last entries are Sheafmonth 416 and the author knows nothing of what follows. Canon: Book One Ch14 and Ch16 (the Ashlane, a lane of coopers; the Bell Yard; 'he had lived near the works and the works had started at the end of his own street'), Ch16 and Ch17 (the Cloister's charitable choir and its choir-mistress, unnamed here), Ch18 (the Office's three questions; the requisition for small clear voices is echoed only by the clerks' polite question about 'the voice', which the midwife misreads as fussiness). Series Bible Part IV (the Narrow: a screaming child calls the hounds and a child who does not cry is a door left open; hymns bring hounds) and Part V (412, the Screaming Year). Umber's 410 account (batch A, lib_a_what_is_written) of the Office's 'great register of the Woods ... by name and voice and age'. Vol II Realm VII (Grove speech warm and full of endearments; the pools that remember). The lamp-man's boy who marries in 416 is Kitto Lowry of lib_g_lamp_book, unnamed here. Names grepped in js/, story/ and the other batches: Grisel, Imrie, Petronel, Bede, Columb, Sabra (no hits; Oriel was rejected as too near Coriel). title: The Little Grove Primer
author: set for the Moot schools of Whisper-Grove; written in by two children of the Carters' Yard
year: 413 SR (new edition, with the Lesson for Quiet); written in until 416
origin: printed at Whisper-Grove for the Moot schools
summary: The alphabet, a counting rhyme and the courtesies every Grove child learned, in a copy passed from an older sister to her little brother, with their pencil in the margins.
text: On the flyleaf, in a careful round hand: This book belongs to Blanche Clough, of the Carters' Yard, Whisper-Grove, the Spectral Woods, the World. Under it, in pencil, much larger: AND NOW TO WILMOT CLOUGH BECAUSE BLANCHE IS TOO BIG FOR IT.
THE LITTLE GROVE PRIMER. Letters, Counting and Courtesies, for the Small Ones of the Moot Schools. New edition, with the Lesson for Quiet.

To the dame, or the mother, or the big sister: go slowly. A letter a day is plenty. Say each one aloud, softly, and let the small one say it after you. That is how the Grove has always learned anything.
THE LETTERS.

A is the Ashlane, steep as a stair; say good morning to all who are there. B is the Basin, long and still, with lanterns upon it, as many as will. C is the Canopy, taller than tall; it keeps the whole Grove, the great and the small.
D is for Dearling, and so are you. Beside it, in Blanche's pencil: NOT WILMOT. Beside that, in a worse pencil: IS.

E is the Evening, the lamps are alight; the lighter goes round, and the Grove says goodnight. F is the Fountain: look, but don't paddle. G is the Grove, and the Grove is home. H is your Hand: give it to whoever is smaller.

I is the Ink, and you will spill it. J is the Jug, and you will spill that too. K is the Kettle; ask before you touch. L is the Lamp-man: if you are lost, wait by his lamp. M is the Moot-house, where the grown people talk, and talk, and talk.
N is your Name. Say it clearly when you are asked, and ask other people theirs.

O is for Others; there are always others. P is the Pool, which remembers. You may look at what it shows you, but do not stare, for it is somebody else's and you would not like them staring at yours. Q is for Quiet, the gentle kind. R is the Rain on the willows.
S is for Singing, as soft as you can. T is for Thank you, said every time. U is for Up the steps, and no running. V is your Voice: keep your small one for indoors. W is the Willow, silver and long.
X is the mark that grown people make when they cannot write their names. You will never need it. Y is for Yesterday, which the Grove keeps for you. Z is the sound of a small one asleep.

COUNTING, for the plaza steps. One step, two steps, down to the plaza; three steps, four steps, hold your sister; five, six, the basin's brim; seven, eight, don't fall in; nine, ten, up again; and eleven lamps in the Bell Yard, lit one by one, and the lamp-man says goodnight when he is done.

COURTESIES. When you meet an old one in the lane, say: good morning, little mother; good morning, little father. When you are given a thing, say: you are kind. When you do not know a person's name, ask it. It is not rude in the Grove to ask a name. It is rude not to.

IF YOU ARE LOST. Do not run. Stand under the nearest lamp, because the lighter will come by. When a grown person asks you, say three things, clearly: your name, your street, and your mother's name. Then you will be home before your supper is cold.

THE LESSON FOR QUIET, new in this edition by order of the Moot. Since the Screaming Year there are things beyond the Woods that come to loud singing. They have not come here. We teach this so that they never need to. Skip it in the yard until you know it: Too loud brings the hounds, too still brings the Hush. So sing in the middle, and sing it soft, and never sing in a rush.

And this, which is harder. If somebody calls your name from the dark or the mist, and you cannot see their face, do not answer. Not even if it sounds like your mam. Go to the nearest lamp, and wait for the lighter, and he will take you home, and your mam will not be cross.
In the margin, in Blanche's pencil: Wilmot answered Mam from the privy and got smacked. It WAS Mam.
NOW WRITE YOUR OWN NAME, as big and as clear as you can, so that everyone will know whose book this is.

BLANCHE CLOUGH, in letters as straight as a fence. Below it, WILMOT CLOUGH, with the C the wrong way round and then crossed out and done again the right way, and the G very large, and a drawing of a lamp on its iron arm.
Well done, dearling. A child who knows her letters, and her name, and her street, can always be brought home.
notes: A copy in use from 413 to 416. Nothing of the Unnaming is known to it; the irony of the last lesson is the reader's alone, and nothing about the children's fate is stated or rendered. Canon: Book One Ch14 and Ch15 (the Weeping Plaza, basin, Moot-house, Bell Yard, the Ashlane; the carters' yard with its carts; the old lamplighter on Bell Yard), Ch16 and Ch20 (Grove children's names sewn into their clothes; Annet Sowerby's 'which home'). Vol II Realm VII (endearments in Grove speech; 'dearling' and 'little mother' follow lib_f_lantern_on_the_basin; the pools that remember). Vol VII (b) §4 (lanterns on the basin). Eleven lamps on the Bell Yard round agrees with lib_g_lamp_book. Names grepped in js/, story/ and the other batches (Blanche, Wilmot, Clough: no hits; Maudie was rejected as too near Maud in js/house13.js). title: Receipts of the Basin Table
author: Edith Amory, of the Bell Yard; with additions by her daughter Rosamund
summary: A Grove cook's receipts for the feast nights on the Weeping Plaza, with her daughter's notes in the back pages and one receipt that was never written down.
text: Edith Amory, of the Bell Yard, her receipts. To Rosamund when I am done with them, and not before, and she is not to lend them to her aunt.

The Grove is not a hot-kitchen people. On the feast nights we eat out of doors, on the plaza steps, in the damp, and so we eat things that are good cold and better shared. Everything in this book can be carried in one hand, because on a feast night the other hand is always busy.
One rule before any receipt. Never cook a fish out of a remembering pool. It is perfectly wholesome, and it tastes of somebody else's supper.

LANTERN CAKES, for the night the water is highest. A plain dough of fine flour and butter, one egg to the pound, rolled thin and folded three times and rolled again, and cut in rounds the size of a child's palm, with a thumb-print in each for a spoon of plum or bramble. Bake them the afternoon before, because nobody has a minute on the day. They are for eating on the steps while you wait your turn at the basin. A child with a lantern cake in one hand will not drop his lantern in the water with the other. I have never known it fail, except with Rosamund, once.

STRAW-BOX BROTH. There are no fires on the plaza, by order of the Moot, on account of the colonnade. So the broth is made at noon: barley, leeks, the end of a ham, and a fistful of the cress that grows at the edges of the clean pools, the ones that show you nothing but your own nose. Bring it to a hard boil, then put the whole pot into a box packed with hay, a blanket over the top, and carry it down. At the ninth hour of the evening it will still take the skin off a tongue.

MOOT PASTIES. The Moot sits from the second hour of the afternoon until it stops, and it never stops. Make the pastry short and the filling dry, so they can be eaten on the benches without crumbs or noise: chestnut and mushroom, a little onion, a good deal of pepper. The householders say they come to the Moot for the business. They come for the pasties.

THE REMEMBERING LOAF, for Canopy, the first Memoryday of Ashfall. A round wheat loaf, glazed with milk. Before it goes into the oven, score the top once for each of the house who has gone, and say the name as you draw the knife, not loud. At supper the loaf is broken, never cut, and everyone at the table eats a piece of everyone. Light the candle in the window facing in, so that the light is for the house and not for the street. This year we scored it six times: my mother; my father; my husband's two brothers; the little one before Rosamund; and old Nan, who was nobody's but ate at our table for thirty years and is entitled.

MY CANOPY CAKE, for after the loaf. A dark cake: treacle, ground chestnut, dried pears chopped small, an egg, and the spice. I keep the spice in my head. A cook keeps one thing in her head or she is only a book.
Here the hand changes. The rest is in a younger, faster hand, with the letters leaning forward.

412. Mother says the pears are not as red this year as when she was a girl, and the plums have no bloom on them. I cannot see it. She says I will when I am old, and that this is the whole trouble with being old: you can see everything that has gone.

413. Lantern Night. Mother too tired for the steps, so I took the cakes down alone and gave them out along the basin. A small boy from the Carters' Yard asked whether he might have two, because his sister was too big for hers. I gave him two. His sister, who was not too big for anything, took one off him at once.

414. Mother died in Thawmonth, in her chair by the window, with her shawl on and her feet on the fender. I am told it is a good way to go and I am sure it is. The Echo will have caught her. She was never one to wander off.

Canopy, 414. I scored the loaf seven times. My hand went on the seventh, and I had to stop and start again. Broken, not cut. Everybody at the table had a piece of everybody, and that included her. I lit the candle facing in and sat up with it, which you are not meant to do, and nobody told me not to.

415. The Lantern Night. Water higher than any year I remember. I made her cakes and they were right. The broth was right. A woman from the Reach was on the steps, lodging with the Lantrys, a lantern on her knees she could not set down; I gave her a cake and she ate it without noticing, which is the best thing a cake can do.

Canopy, 415. I have tried her cake four times this year. The treacle, the chestnut, the pears: all right. The spice is wrong. It is not cinnamon and it is not clove and it is not the pepper off the Organum carts. She never wrote it down, and I never asked, because she was always going to be in the kitchen.
So when I find it, I will keep it in my head, the way she did, and not write it down. Whoever has this book after me will have to come to the Bell Yard and ask.
notes: Written 405 to 415, before the Unnaming. Canon: Book One Ch14 (the Weeping Plaza, its colonnade and basin, the Moot-house, the Bell Yard). Vol VII §4 and Vol VII (b) §3 to §4 (Canopy on the first Memoryday of Ashfall, the remembering of the dead, candles in windows facing in; the Drowned Lanterns on the night the Grove's water is highest). Vol I §1.9 (the Echo catching the dead of the Woods in the Weeping Canopy, 'what the old faith called heaven'), used only as household belief. Series Bible Part III (everyone over thirty remembers when red was redder) and Part VI (reflecting pools show strangers' memories). The Reach woman lodging with the Lantrys is Tabitha Fernly of lib_f_lantern_on_the_basin (415), unnamed; the boy from the Carters' Yard and his sister are the Clough children of lib_g_grove_primer, unnamed. Names grepped in js/, story/ and the other batches (Edith, Rosamund, Amory: no hits). title: Letters in a Blue Ribbon
author: Cressida Tilney, copy-clerk to the Moot, and Corbet Ansty, journeyman pipe-voicer; bound by her
summary: Two years of letters between a Moot clerk in Whisper-Grove and a Grove-born pipe-voicer working in the Organum, and a proposal she will only answer aloud.
text: The Organum, Reedmonth 414. Cressida. I am here and I am alive and I have not been run over by a Justiciar, though it was close on the second day. You will want to know what it is like. It is loud. Not the way the Grove is loud on a Moot night, all of us murmuring at once; loud the way the inside of a bell is loud. The towers are pipes and the streets are ranks, and when the Synod speaks the whole city plays, and you feel it in your back teeth and in the soles of your boots. I am in the east rank under a master who has voiced pipes for forty years and thinks I am an idiot. You said you might write. Might is a word the Moot uses when it means no. Corbet.

Whisper-Grove, Longsun 414. Corbet Ansty. I am writing, which is not the same as might and not the same as yes. The Moot sat nine hours on Massday over the paint on the colonnade, whether white or the old grey, and I copied every word, and at the end they agreed to sit again. I enclose nothing. You may imagine a pressed willow-leaf if it helps. C. T.

The Organum, Firstfruit 414. C. T. Thank you for the willow-leaf. It is the finest I have ever imagined. You asked, or you did not ask but I will tell you, what a voicer does. A pipe is made to speak one note. It does not know which until you tell it, and you tell it by cutting the mouth, a hair at a time, and listening, and cutting again. Every pipe has one note it was made for, and when you have found it you know, because it stops arguing. My master says I cut too fast. He is right. I think it is because I am homesick. I miss the quiet. I miss the pools showing me somebody's breakfast. Will you do a thing for me? On the Lantern Night, set one for my grandfather, Old Ansty of the Cloister road. I cannot get leave, and somebody ought to say him. Corbet.

Whisper-Grove, Ashfall 414. Corbet. I set it. I said his name on the basin, and the people beside me said it after me, and so did the people beside them, a long way down the water, so your grandfather is now a public matter and will be discussed. It was a good lantern. I made it myself, and it went out straight and did not tip. Canopy was quiet. We scored the loaf at home and I lit the candle facing in. I have kept your letters, all four. Do not let that go to your head; I keep the Moot's minutes too. C.

The Organum, Stillmonth 415. Cressida Tilney. I have voiced eleven pipes since I wrote last and every one of them stopped arguing. I have got better at listening. So I am going to say it, as plainly as I can, in ink, because ink is what I have. Marry me. Corbet.

Whisper-Grove, Thawmonth 415. Corbet. No. Read the rest of this before you throw yourself off a tower. A thing written in a letter can be taken back; it is only ink, and ink is cheap, I buy it for the Moot by the jar. In the Grove a thing that matters is said aloud, on the water, in front of other people, so that it is heard and kept. You know this. You were named on a pool like the rest of us. So come home and say it on the basin steps, aloud, and I will answer you there, aloud, and the whole Grove may say it after us if it likes. That is not no, you fool. It is not yet. C.

The Organum, Seedmonth 415. C. My master will not give me leave until my journeyman year is out, which by his count is Sheafmonth of next year, and by mine is a hundred years. Will you wait? I have bought nothing yet, because I do not know what you would like, and because if I buy it I will look at it every night and cut my pipes too fast. Corbet.

Whisper-Grove, Dustmonth 415. Corbet. I will wait, and I will not be gracious about it. News, since you are homesick. The fuller's girl in the Ashlane had twins, and the second would not breathe until the first shouted at it, and the whole lane is telling it, and Grisel Imrie is pretending she is not proud. The lamp-men voted to keep lighting, which they do every year, and Old Lowry made a speech, which he does every year. The pools are high. I copy the Moot and I read your letters on the gallery at noon, where the light is good. Nobody up there can see what I am reading, which is just as well, because it is mostly the same letter. C.

The Organum, Lambmonth 416. Cressida. The city played for three hours yesterday because the Synod was speaking, and I stood in the rank with my hands over my ears like a boy and could not hear a single word of what it said. You never can. That is the thing about this place: everything is said aloud and nobody can make it out. In the Grove you can hear a person drop a spoon across the plaza, and you always know whose spoon it was. I have been away too long. Corbet.

The Organum, Firstfruit 416. C. T. My master has signed my papers. He shook my hand and told me I still cut too fast and that I will be a good voicer in about thirty years. I have bought a ribbon, blue, because you said once that you liked the blue ones on the Moot rolls, and I bought it without looking at it so as not to cut my pipes too fast. I will be home before Canopy. I will come down the Moot-house steps and stand on the basin's edge and say it, aloud, in front of the whole Grove, and you will have to answer aloud, Cressida Tilney, and everybody will hear. Corbet.

On the last leaf, in her hand: Bound by me, Sheafmonth 416, with the ribbon off my good hat, so that I shall have them all in one place when he comes, and can read him back every word if he tries to take any of it back. He is due before Canopy. I have been practising my answer up in the muniment store, where nobody can hear me. It is one word. I have had it ready since Reedmonth of 414.
notes: Written 414 to 416, the last leaf in Sheafmonth 416, before the Unnaming of Ashfall 416; the author knows nothing of what follows, and the book says nothing of either writer's fate. title: The Plaza and the Canopy, as the Old People Tell It
author: Carrick Thackray, clerk to the Moot of Whisper-Grove
summary: The Moot's own clerk writes down what the Grove believes about its great tree, its drowned-lamp basin and its quarrelsome Moot, giving both versions wherever the old people disagree.
text: Carrick Thackray, clerk to the Moot, wrote this. For Joliffe, my grandson, who asked me how old the plaza was and would not take very for an answer.

The Moot asked me at its Sheafmonth sitting to set down a history of the plaza and the Canopy before the old people who know it are all gone, which is true, and was rudely put. I have done my best. Where the old people agree, I have written it plain. Where they disagree, which is everywhere, I have written both, and the reader may choose. I am a clerk, not a judge. The Moot pays me by the page and not by the verdict.

OF THE CANOPY. From any street in the Grove, if you look up past the roofs, you will see it: wood and crystal grown together into one thing, silver at the root and pale as ice where it goes up into the mist, so tall that nobody has ever seen the top. Nobody has ever seen it grow, and nobody remembers it shorter.

The old people say it was the first willow, and that the Grove grew up around it because people like to live near something that remembers. They say its roots run under the whole of the Woods. The scribes up at the House of the Veil say the roots come down through their own cellars, a long day's walk from here, and the scribes do not tell lies, though they do not tell much else either.

The old people say also that when one of the Grove dies, the Echo catches them, and the Canopy keeps them. That is why we keep Canopy, on the first Memoryday of Ashfall, with a candle facing in. My grandmother said that on a still night you could hear them if you put your ear to a root, saying their names over to themselves, the way children say their letters. I tried it when I was eight. I heard my own blood going. My grandmother said that was the same thing.

The Church says otherwise. The Church's man, who is a decent fellow and eats with the Moot on feast days, says that the Canopy is the Spire of Memory, one of the eight that sing the laws of the world, and that it sings the law by which things are remembered, and that the dead are with the Pure Note and nowhere else. I have written down both. I do not choose.

The pools are the Canopy's too, or so the old people say: it drinks from them, and dreams into them, and that is why a pool will sometimes show you a stranger's kitchen, or a stranger's morning. Children are taught to look and not to stare. It is somebody else's, and you would not want them staring at yours.

OF THE PLAZA. It is the size of four fields, all white marble, with a colonnade on three sides and the Moot-house on the fourth. The old people say the Moot-house was put on the fourth side so that the Moot should always have the whole Grove in front of it, and the whole Grove should always be able to see whether the Moot was awake.

It was laid, they say, in the time of the crowns, before the Reckoning, by masons who were paid in nothing but supper for forty years, because the Grove had nothing else to pay them in. That is why a Grove mason will still not take a fee for mending the plaza, only his supper, which the Moot finds very convenient and does not mention.

Down the middle runs the basin, cut long and shallow for the lamps. Here the old people disagree. Some say the first lantern was set by a woman whose son went out into the Woods and did not come back; she put a lamp on the water so he could find his way, and said his name aloud, and her neighbours said it after her. He did not come back. The lamps did, every year after, on the night the water is highest. Others say the custom is older than the basin, and that the basin was cut for it and not the other way about, and the scribes at the House take this side, and will show you nothing to prove it.

OF THE MOOT. Every householder may sit. Anyone may speak once on a question, and twice if they are very old. Nothing is decided until the lamp-man has lit the lamp on the Moot-house door, which is an old rule and a good one, because it means nothing is ever decided in a hurry. The longest Moot in the rolls sat nine days on whether the plaza steps should have a rail. It ruled that they should not, because a rail would spoil the steps for sitting on. Nobody has fallen off them since that anybody will admit to.

Above the hall is the gallery, where the light is best, and behind it the muniment store, where the rolls are kept, tied in blue. Below is the cellar, where the Moot keeps its cider in a barrel made by a cooper of the Ashlane. The barrel has not leaked in fourteen years, and the cooper is insufferable about it.

Along the west wall the Moot keeps the town's books: anything a householder leaves to the Moot, and the books that travellers bring. Long ago two houses of the Ashlane fell out over whose family book should stand on the top shelf, and the Moot sat three nights on it, and ruled that the town's books should be shelved by size and not by name, so that no house's book stands above another's: the tall ones at the back, the small ones on the left. The clerk shelves them. I have shelved them for thirty-one years. It is the most restful work in the Grove, and it is the only ruling of the Moot that nobody has ever asked to have reversed.

OF THE HOUSE. The scribes of the Veil keep their House in the deep Woods and come down to us when there is something to write. For as long as the rolls go back, the Moot gave the House its vellum, and the House copied the Moot's rolls fair once in every generation and kept the copy, against fire. Since the Veil was taken into the Synod's Office the scribes come with grey ink, and are very polite, and do not stay for supper. We liked them.

That is the history, or as much of it as the old people would agree to let me write. The Moot has met on this plaza for longer than anybody can count. In all that time it has never once agreed about anything, and it has never once failed to meet. I think that is what a town is.

Joliffe. When you are a householder, go to the Moot. Sit at the back. Speak once a year. And when the Moot rises, put the books back the way you found them: the tall ones at the back, by size, not by name.

title: The Commonplace Book of the Scribe Styled Bistre
author: Bistre, scribe of the House
origin: the House of the Silent Veil, the Spectral Woods
summary: Forty years of things one Veil scribe liked: receipts for ink, a prayer for Memoryday, sayings worth stealing, and small observations from a cold room.
text: Bistre. The designation given me from the ink-cupboard by the Prior's hand, Stillmonth 371. The last Bistre was an old man who left me a cracked horn, a good penknife, and the habit of humming while he ruled a page, which the duty-scribe asks me every week to break.
Things worth keeping, copied as I find them. This is not a record. Records go on vellum. This is only what I liked.

THE INK OF THE HOUSE. Oak-galls, from the oaks along the Organum road, because there are none in the Woods. Crush them, do not grind them, and steep them nine days in rainwater. Never pool water: the old scribes say pool water makes an ink that remembers what it would rather have written. Green copperas, a thumb's weight to the pint, which turns it as black as the second note. Gum, until it hangs from the quill and thinks about it before it falls. Stir with a willow stick. Never with iron.

LAMPBLACK, for the pitched hand. The soot of the east stove, scraped on the last day of the month when the desks are done with vinegar. Work it with gum and one drop of honey, so that it runs in the long held strokes and does not break.

The three rules, which every scribe knows and which I copy here only because a commonplace book without them looks undressed. Write what happened. Write who it happened to. Do not comfort yourself in the margin.

A thing said by the Registrar of the Office to an apprentice, in my hearing, in the year 405: Rule the page before you write on it. A margin is not decoration. A margin is the place where you are not permitted to put your own opinion, and leaving it empty is the discipline of the whole trade. I copy it because it is good, and because I wish I had said it, and because I have been putting my own opinion in the margins of this book for thirty-four years and have no intention of stopping.

BEFORE THE PAGE ON MEMORYDAY, said under the breath on the stair, with the lamp. You who are on this page: I am not the one who forgets you. I am only the one who comes. Hear your names, and hold them a while longer. I will be back in eight days.

There are no birds in the Woods. I have looked for forty years. A novice from the Peaks asked me where they had gone. I said they had never come. She said that was worse, and she was right, and I have liked her ever since.

The pool under the House is highest on the night the Grove sets its lanterns. From the north windows you can see, a long way off through the willows, a glow on the mist where they are putting their names on the water. We set ours from the steps under the arch, one each, and say them in the flat voice, and the pool takes them round the bend and out of sight.

Vinegar day. The whole floor smells of it, and of tallow, and of wet wool. A novice asked me today to describe the smell to her, because she had just come and could not tell it from damp. I could not. I said she would know it in a winter. She asked what I meant. I said: you will know it the way you know your own name, which is to say you will never once think about it until somebody takes it away.

THE OFFICE'S GREY INK, which comes by the cask and is free. It does not bite the vellum. It sits on it, like oil on a pool. It is good for registers that are to be read within the year and poor for registers that are to be read in a thousand. I have written to the Office to say so, in grey ink, as required.
FOR AN INKY HAND. Sorrel juice, pumice, and patience. Nothing takes out the second knuckle. Wear it.
A thing the Prior said to a weeping novice, which I copy without his leave: The House does not ask you not to feel. It asks you not to write it down. Feel all you like. Feel it on the stairs.

412, the Screaming Year. My minium has gone brown on the page, and I will swear on the Rule that it is the same pot. The Prior says it is the light that is wrong, not the ink. A scribe from the south wing says the light is wrong everywhere and the ink knows it. I have written down both and I do not choose.

413. Sent down to the stacks by the roster, four of us, as the roster says. We came up quiet, as one does. The Rule lets me write this much and no more: it is not silent down there, and it is not sad. It is like standing in a crowded room where everyone is being introduced.

414. My hand shakes in the cold now. The duty-scribe has moved me nearer the east stove, which I resent and enjoy in equal parts. I have copied the three rules once more below, in the pitched hand, slowly, to see whether I still can.
Here follow the three rules in the old notation: small even marks, each line falling at its end, the held strokes long and unbroken.
Still can. Whoever has this book after me: it is not a record. Read it anyway. It is only what one scribe liked, in a cold room, for forty years, and I liked all of it.
notes: Spans c. 371 to 414, so before the vellum was taken (416) and before the Unnaming. Canon: Vol V §3 (the House, the scribes' own name; the scriptorium; a stove at each end, the east stove lit by the duty-scribe; the motto in pitched notation; the Office took the vellum to the Organum), Book One Ch14 and Ch22 (desks cleaned with vinegar on the last day of every month; cold stone, tallow, wet wool, vinegar), Ch15 (the three rules, quoted exactly; ink to the second knuckle), Ch22 epigraph (Quist's precept 'Rule the page before you write on it ...', said to a nineteen-year-old apprentice c. 405; quoted exactly and attributed only to 'an apprentice'), Series Bible Part III (the catechism: sin is the second note) and Part V (c. 300 SR the Veil absorbed as the Office; 412 the Screaming Year; red was redder). title: Exercises in the Pitched Hand
author: a novice of the House, his name scraped from the cover; corrected in minium by the scribe styled Woad
origin: the House of the Silent Veil, the Spectral Woods
summary: A homesick novice's exercise book, learning the Veil's notation one mark at a time, with his master's red corrections and one long argument about the motto over the door.
text: On the cover, a name in a boy's hand, scraped away with a penknife until the vellum is thin. Beneath it, in red: Novices do not write their names on House paper. You will have it back at the door. W.
EXERCISES IN THE PITCHED HAND. For the novice at the fourth desk, south side. Set by Woad.

THE FIRST LESSON: THE MARKS. The pitched hand does not write a word as it is spelled. It writes a word as it is said: how high, how long, and where the breath falls. The common hand keeps what a name means. The pitched hand keeps how it sounds in the mouth that said it. That is why it is ours, and why it is slow.

The line, which is a sound held. The hook up, which is a rise. The hook down, which is a fall. The dot, which is a rest; a rest is not nothing, and it is written. The tie, for two sounds that may not be parted. The stroke through, which is a breath taken. Five heights, ruled faint, and the marks sit on them like birds on a rail, if you have ever seen a bird, which here you will not.
Below, in the boy's hand, a page of marks copied over and over, line, line, hook down, dot, and in red at the foot: Your dots are blots. A rest is small. Make it small.
THE SECOND LESSON: HEAR AND WRITE. I will say a word at the door. Write what you heard, not what you know.
Bread. Willow. Water. Good morning.

In red, beside the last: You wrote good morning rising at the end, the way they say it in the villages, because that is how your mother says it. I said it flat. Write what you heard. Your mother is not in this room.
Beneath that, in the boy's hand, small: I know.

THE VOICE FOR ENTRIES. When you read an entry aloud, read it flat and clear and unhurried, the way a person reads a will. The voice for entries does not rise and does not fall. It is not yours to colour. The name has its own colour. Leave it alone.

On the facing page, in the boy's hand, a list: It is very cold. There are no birds. The stove smokes until the third bell. I miss the noise of the mill. I am not allowed to write this in this book. Beneath it, in red: No, you are not. I have read it, so it is done. Turn the page.

THE THIRD LESSON: THE MOTTO. Over the round arch, cut in the stone in our notation: What is written is not lost. Seven sounds. You walked under them on your first morning and could not read them. By the end of this book you will be able to read them, and write them, and you will never walk under that arch again without hearing them.
First attempt, in the boy's hand. In red beneath: You have put a hook up on lost. You are asking a question. It is not a question.
Second attempt. In red: Better. The tie on written is broken. Do not part what may not be parted.

Third attempt. In red: You have put a dot after not. Why? Below it, the boy: Because I wanted to stop before lost. And in red: So, I expect, did the scribe who cut it over the arch. He did not. Neither will you.
Fourth to eleventh attempts, filling two pages. The red marks get fewer. One is only a tick. One says: The rise has crept back. You are still asking.

At the foot of the eleventh page, very small, in the pitched hand and not in any exercise: a name, three sounds, the last one falling. It is not struck through. Beside it in red: This one is well made. W.

THE FOURTH LESSON: A NAME HEARD AT A DOOR. When you are sworn you will stand a little way off from things, with a board on your arm, and people will tell you their names because they are frightened, or because they are dying, or because nobody else is listening. You will write each one as it was said, the fear in it and the accent and the cough, so that whoever reads it in a thousand years hears that person and not you. Practise on me.
Below, the boy's attempt at the master's own designation, Woad, said at a door. In red: That is very like. You have caught my cold.
The last page. The motto once more, in the boy's best hand: the line held, the tie unbroken, no dot before lost, and the last sound falling to the bottom of the ruling and stopping there.
In red, beneath it: Kept. You may have a designation in the spring. It is not a question. Write it always as if you knew.
notes: Set in 388, long before the Unnaming. Canon: Vol V §3 (the House; the motto over the round arch in the Veil's pitched notation; the scriptorium's sloped desks; the stove), Book One Ch14 and Ch16 (reading names 'flat and clear and unhurried, in the voice of a person reading a will'; a scribe's last-thing-said 'that I could hear from the door'), Vol V §3 (the voice for entries), Vol II Realm VII (no birds in the Woods). The idea that the pitched hand keeps how a name sounds as well as what it is follows Vol II Appendix D ('Signatures / identity is pitch', seeded from Book One) and Umber's 'by name and voice and age' (lib_a_what_is_written), and states nothing about cores or pressing. Consistent with lib_e_veil_rule (the novice's name given up and returned at the door; designations of colour or creature) and lib_a_what_is_written (designations from the ink-cupboard); lib_h_daybook's 'stove lit ... smoked until the third' bell. The novice is a boy and is not Sable. title: Meditations on the Keeping of Names
author: Orpiment, scribe of the House
origin: the House of the Silent Veil, the Spectral Woods
summary: An old Veil scribe's private meditations on her calling, written in the last years of the House, as her own colour fades and the registers are taken away.
text: These are not entries. Nothing here happened to anyone but me. I keep them in the drawer of my desk, under the blotter, and if the Prior finds them he may burn them in the east stove, which is what it is for.

THE FIRST. ON THE CURVE. The Rule says the world forgets on a curve, steep at first and then slow, and that the House stands at the bottom of it with a cup. I have been thinking about the cup. It is a very small thing to hold under a curve that long. A novice once asked me what happens to the names that miss it. I told her that was why we must never miss. She went away satisfied. I did not.

THE SECOND. ON MY OWN NAME. I gave my name into the House forty-four years ago. It was written once in the Prior's hand and sealed and laid in the cabinet, and I have not missed it, and I am told that not missing it is the proof that it is safe. Some evenings I go and stand by the cabinet. Not to open it; it is sealed. The way you stand outside a room where someone you love is asleep, to hear them breathing.

THE THIRD. ON MY COLOUR. Orpiment is the brightest yellow in the ink-cupboard, and a poison. We grind it wet, with a cloth over the mouth. The scribe who had it before me died very old, so it is a slow poison, or a courteous one. Since the Screaming Year it is less yellow. Not on the page only: in the shell, in the cupboard, under my hand. Everyone over thirty says the same of every colour, and the young ones look at us kindly. I find I mind this more than I can account for. A designation is not a name. And yet I have answered to it for forty-four years, and it is going out like a lamp.

THE FOURTH. ON MEMORYDAY. Tonight it was my turn. I went down with the lamp to the lower hall and read the page aloud, flat and unhurried, from where the last scribe stopped. I do not know to whom I read it. Nobody in the House knows; the Rule says only that it is done. I read it the way you read to a child who has fallen asleep halfway through: you finish the chapter anyway, in case.

THE FIFTH. ON THE STACKS. Eleven times down by the roster, and I have kept the Rule each time and written nothing of what is heard there. I will set down only what I felt, which the Rule does not mention, because nobody who wrote the Rule thought it needed saying. I felt expected.

THE SIXTH. ON A WORD. The Office's clerks came again to count the shelves. They wore gloves to touch the registers, and they did not read a page. One of them, a pleasant young man, called what was on the shelves units. He was not being cruel. He did not know there was another word. I have been turning it over for a month. A unit is a thing that may be counted and not missed. A name is a thing that is missed. The whole of the House, eleven hundred years of it, is the distance between those two words, and I do not think it is a long distance, and I do not think it is getting longer.

THE SEVENTH. ON THE VELLUM. It went down the hill today in four wagons. The pool took a wheel and they spent the afternoon getting it out, and the whole House stood at the windows and watched and did not help. The registers are to be kept in the Organum, they say, drier than they have ever been. I believe them. I have never in my life believed anything that comforted me less.

The desks are clean. There is nothing to copy. One pen in the north row is still moving, and nobody has stopped it. I have been sitting at my own desk with my pen dry, listening to it, the way you listen to rain on a roof you are not sure of.

THE EIGHTH. ON TAKING AND KEEPING. The Office has asked for scribes to go down to the Grove with boards and take names for the great register, and I have been chosen, being quick and old and having nothing on my desk. I have taken names all my life. I have stood a little way off from fevers and floods and once a town on fire, and written down who it happened to. That was keeping. I do not know yet what this is. The letter says register. The letter is very well ruled.

THE NINTH. Ashfall, 416. Tomorrow I go down the hill with a board on my arm. Write what happened. Write who it happened to. Do not comfort yourself in the margin. I have kept the third rule for forty-four years and I am going to break it once, here, at the end of my own book, where nobody will read it: I am afraid, and I do not know of what, and I would give my colour to be wrong.
If I do not come back up the hill, whoever has this desk: the names were never ours. We only kept the door on the latch.
notes: Written 413 to Ashfall 416, ending the night before the author goes to Whisper-Grove; nothing about the Unnaming itself is described, and her fate is not stated.
